title: Linear regression
story:
Least squares is the oldest method in this track and still the first thing to reach for, and its origin is a good illustration of what invention means in mathematics.

Legendre published it in 1805, in a book on determining the orbits of comets, and gave it the name it still has. What is striking on reading him is how little justification he offers for squaring. It is convenient — the minimisation has a closed form and a unique answer — and he notes that for repeated direct observations of one unknown it returns the arithmetic mean, which is reassuring but is not an argument that squares are correct. The method spread anyway, and fast: within about a decade it was standard in astronomy and geodesy across France, Italy and Prussia.

Then in 1809 Gauss discussed the method, mentioned Legendre, and added that he had been using it himself since 1795 — our principle, of which we have made use since the year 1795. Legendre was badly offended and wrote to him on 31 May 1809 that priority is established only by publication. Gauss never replied. His position was that he cared about being first to discover rather than first to publish, and that the idea was simple enough that others must have used it before him too. His evidence was thin: his computational notes were lost, and only Olbers put anything in print, a footnote in 1816 saying Gauss had shown him the method in 1802.

The fair reading is that both contributions are real and they are different in kind. Legendre published the algebraic procedure and it was adopted. Gauss did the deeper thing, connecting least squares to probability and the normal distribution, which Laplace then formalised in 1812 — and that connection is what turns the method from a convenient recipe into an estimator with properties you can state. The dispute is worth knowing because it is a clean case of the two ways a thing gets invented, and because the question it obscures is the interesting one: why squares at all?

The honest answer is that squares were chosen for tractability and justified afterwards. Under normally distributed errors the least-squares fit is the maximum-likelihood estimate, which is a genuine justification and is conditional on an assumption about the errors. Where that assumption fails, the choice bites: because the penalty grows with the square of the discrepancy, one distant point pulls the line further than many nearby ones, and the fit reports itself as confidently as ever.

problem.name: Least squares
problem.shape: Several observations bear on the same unknown quantities and disagree, and you need one answer plus a rule for producing it that does not depend on preference.
tell: measurements of the same thing do not agree
a relationship is being summarised by a straight line
the errors are assumed symmetric without anyone checking
a small number of points lie far from the rest
problem.move: Minimise the sum of squared discrepancies when the errors are roughly symmetric and free of extreme values, and know that you are choosing maximum likelihood under normal errors when you do. Where extremes are present, minimise absolute deviations or use a robust loss instead, and always look at the residuals rather than only the summary of the fit.
problem.invariant: The fitted line is the one minimising squared discrepancy, which makes it the maximum-likelihood estimate exactly when the errors are normally distributed. Everything the method claims beyond a best fit rests on that condition.
problem.breaks: The squared penalty makes influence grow with distance, so a single point far from the others moves the fit more than many points near it, and the summary statistics do not reveal that this happened. Robustness and tractability are traded directly: absolute deviations resist extremes and lose the closed form and the uniqueness.

cost.time: a closed-form solution, which is the property that made it usable with pen and paper in 1805 and keeps it the cheapest baseline available
cost.space: the coefficients, one per feature, which is also why the fitted model is inspectable in a way most of this track is not
cost.beats: minimising absolute deviations, which is more robust to extremes and has no closed form, and eyeballing a line, which has no defensible rule at all

worked.problem: Why minimise the squares of the errors rather than their absolute values?
worked.reasoning:
Historically because it was tractable, and mathematically because of an assumption about the errors that was supplied afterwards. Both halves matter, and the second is the one that decides whether the choice is right for your data.

The tractability came first, and honestly so. Squaring gives a smooth objective with a closed-form solution and a unique minimum. Legendre offered little more than that in 1805, observing that the rule returns the arithmetic mean when you have repeated direct observations of a single unknown — reassuring, but not an argument that squares are correct. Absolute deviations have no closed form, and in 1805 that difference was decisive.

The justification arrived with Gauss, who connected the method to probability and the normal distribution, and with Laplace, who formalised it in 1812. The result is that under normally distributed errors the least-squares fit is the maximum-likelihood estimate. That is a real argument, and it is conditional: squares are optimal given an assumption about how the errors are distributed, not in general.

What follows is the practical consequence. Squaring makes influence grow with distance, so a point ten units away pulls a hundred times as hard as one a unit away. If the errors really are normal, distant points are rare and that weighting is correct — it is extracting the information such a point carries. If the errors are heavy-tailed, or a few observations are simply wrong, the same weighting hands the fit to the least trustworthy rows, and nothing in the summary statistics says so.

Absolute deviations fix that by making influence constant with distance, which is why they estimate something nearer the median than the mean. The costs are real: no closed form, a solution that need not be unique, and worse efficiency when the errors genuinely are normal. Huber-type losses split the difference, behaving quadratically near zero and linearly in the tails.

So my answer is that squares are the right default and should be a checked default. I would fit with squares, plot the residuals, look for a handful of points doing a disproportionate share of the work, and refit with a robust loss to see whether the coefficients move. If they move a lot, the squared fit was describing those few points.

problem.practice: Fit a line by least squares, then move one point far from the others and refit. Record how far the line travelled. Then fit the same two datasets by minimising absolute deviations and compare how much that fit moved instead.

beats.broke: Several measurements bear on the same unknown and disagree, and you need one answer together with a rule for combining them that does not depend on which measurement you prefer.
beats.fix: Take the line minimising the sum of squared discrepancies — published in 1805, named there, and adopted across astronomy and geodesy within a decade because it has a closed form and a unique solution.
beats.cost: Squaring was chosen for tractability and justified afterwards, by the connection to the normal distribution that makes it the maximum-likelihood estimate — so influence grows with the square of distance, and one far point pulls the line further than many near ones.

interview.q: Why minimise the squares of the errors rather than their absolute values?
interview.trap: Answering that squares keep everything positive. So does the absolute value; the real reasons are the closed form and the fact that squares are maximum likelihood under normally distributed errors, which is a conditional justification rather than a general one.
